awd_titl_txt: RAPID: Nitrogen Oxide Measurements to Support Dynamics of Emissions, Nucleation, and Aerosols to predict Land-atmosphere-climate Interactions (DENALI) Field Campaign in Alaska
awd_abstract_narration:
This RAPID project will support the participation of US scientists in a field campaign named the Dynamics of Emissions, Nucleation, and Aerosols to predict Land-atmosphere-climate Interactions (DENALI). This campaign is being led by the University of Helsinki in Finland. The project features a comparative analysis of biogenic volatile organic compound emissions between the boreal forests in Hyytiälä and those in North America. Differences in  the biogenic emissions from these forests can lead to differences in oxidation chemistry and new particle formation, with implications for atmospheric composition.

A CAPS NOX-NO2 instrument will be deployed at the Delta Junction site in Alaska from May of 2025 to August of 2025 to supplement the suite of instruments supported by European colleagues. This measurement is important because NOx may significantly influence new particle formation processes. The NOx measurement also will provide a fundamental understanding of the fate of organic peroxy radicals that can affect the formation of highly oxygenated organic molecules (HOMs) in this environment.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project investigated the sources and sinks of nitrogen oxides in the boreal forest near Delta Junction, Alaska. Nitrogen oxides—primarily nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2), collectively called NOx—are important because they influence ozone production, the oxidation of gases emitted by vegetation, and the formation and growth of atmospheric particles. However, relatively few detailed measurements of these processes have been made in the North American Boreal Forest (NABF). This project provided in situ nitrogen oxides (NOx) measurements for the duration of the Dynamics of Emissions, Nucleation, and Aerosols to predict Land-atmosphere-climate Interactions (DENALI) field campaign that took place at the ASCENT research site in Delta Junction Alaska during the summer of 2025. These NOx measurements, in conjunction with other measurements on gas and aerosol phases conducted during DENALI, provided the first ever study focusing on new particle formation in North American Boreal Forrest (NABF).

NOx concentrations at Delta Junction were generally very low. NO typically ranged from 20 to 100 parts per trillion, with a median of approximately 30 parts per trillion. NO2 ranged from near zero to 1.2 parts per billion, with a median of approximately 0.2 parts per billion. NOₓ concentrations at Delta Junction were approximately 30% lower on average than measurements from the Hyytiälä boreal-forest site in Finland, even though the Alaska campaign included periods affected by wildfire smoke. Nevertheless, the daily patterns at the two sites were strongly correlated, suggesting that similar local atmospheric processes control the timing of concentration maxima and minima. These findings indicate that the Delta Junction forest experienced less anthropogenic influence and represents a comparatively clean boreal environment.

Wildfires affected the site during roughly half of the campaign and represented the clearest influence on measured NOx. Median NO and NO2 concentrations were approximately 20% higher during wildfire-influenced periods. Wildfires can supply NOx directly through combustion and can also produce compounds such as peroxyacetyl nitrate and other organic nitrogen compounds that transport reactive nitrogen over long distances before releasing NOₓ.

The project examined whether rainfall stimulated NO emissions from soil microbes. Measurements were separated into dry, stable periods and wetter, recently disturbed periods using the time since the last precipitation event. Although isolated increases occurred after rainfall, NOx concentrations were not statistically different between the two categories. Supporting soil observations from the National Ecological Observatory Network showed that the site has sandy, moderately acidic soil but an unusually small supply of inorganic nitrogen and relatively few nitrifying and denitrifying microorganisms. Together, these results indicate that soil emissions were probably not a major regional source of NOx during the campaign. Combustion sources, including wildfire smoke and smaller contributions from roads or nearby military activities, are more likely sources.

The project advances understanding of atmospheric chemistry in a rapidly changing and fire-sensitive region. Its measurements provide an important benchmark for evaluating atmospheric models and determining how wildfire smoke, vegetation, soil processes, and human activities affect boreal air quality. The combined dataset will also support continued research into how NOx changes the chemistry of organic radicals, the production of highly oxygenated molecules, and the formation and growth of new atmospheric particles. These particles can influence human health, visibility, clouds, and climate, connecting the project’s fundamental atmospheric-chemistry discoveries to broader societal and environmental concerns.
